rv.q: These great mid-century American dramas, with their compassionate emphasis on human frailty, could so easily feel out-of-step with our shriller, narcissistic modern moment – but Frecknall makes them speak anew.
Frecknall turns the tilth on a half-buried play, and digs up something extraordinary.
Shannon is a revelation, too, as the O’Neill self-portrait James ‘Jim’ Tyrone, recycled from his better-known family epic Long Day’s Journey Into Night.
This is a chance to see a challenging American classic with great clarity.
Breathing fresh life and painfully relatable emotion into Eugene O’Neill’s tender, tawdry tragedy of missed connections and unconsummated longing, this riveting revival seethes with unspoken subtext.
Key to this mesmerising production is the tough honesty to their performances and the subtlety with which they reveal the complexity of their characters.
Acting this fine makes it all worthwhile.

Rebecca Frecknall’s latest gorgeous resurrection of a mid-century American gem makes spotlights orbit round her cast on rollercoaster-style rails, capturing every shifting phase of their sub-lunar interactions.
It’s long, bottom-flattening but for the most part, compellingly watchable.
At the centre, Ruth Wilson is a transfixing mixture of earthiness and otherness...

His late work about a big-boned Connecticut farmer’s daughter and a fading alcoholic admirer who struggle to tell the truth about each other is a strange, lumpy affair that takes a very long time to get down to business.
Frecknall is sometimes charged with being too overbearing a director but this production might have benefited from bigger, bolder revisionism.
You're left eavesdropping on life even as Shannon's James gives off the anguished mien of the walking dead.
This is a watchable, entertaining performance of one of the plays that helped shape world theatre and will quickly sell out.

Eugene O’Neill’s final major work, set during the 1920s on a run-down Connecticut farm, brings some star power to Islington’s Almeida with Ruth Wilson paired opposite double Oscar nominee Michael Shannon. David Threlfall and Ruth Wilson in A Moon for the Misbegotten at the Almeida Theatre. Credit Marc Brenner.
This production is padded with star power, courtesy of Ruth Wilson, Michael Shannon and David Threllfall, each of whom delivers a performance worthy of their reputation.
Although the bagginess of the play remains a sticking point, this is a valuable chance to see it delivered with dynamism and no small amount of humour from an ensemble of the very highest quality.
A strong production subdued by the limitations of the play.

Yet this Moon for the Misbegotten doesn’t hang together; it feels too heavy, the words always in the way of the emotions instead of the route to them, and just when you think it is about to explode into something powerful, the momentum ebbs away.
Episodes of Scooby-Doo have better plots than this.

cn.t: Mostly rapturous reviews for Frecknall's revival, with Wilson and Shannon's performances drawing near-universal praise. A few critics find O'Neill's text dated and the pacing sluggish, but most call it spellbinding.
